items.titleEn: Salesforce stock slides as technology outages rattle software sector
items.summaryEn: Buy ServiceNow (NOW). If the market is repricing “enterprise software reliability,” the winners are the platforms with stronger operational track records and mission-critical stickiness. NOW sold off less than CRM and is positioned as the workflow/IT-ops backbone—exactly what companies lean on after disruptions. Second-order setup: as outages spread, IT teams accelerate automation and incident-management spending, which supports NOW demand even while other SaaS names de-rate. Key Risk: A new, widely reported ServiceNow service disruption that breaks the “reliability premium” and triggers further de-rating. Sell Salesforce (CRM). The stock is down hard on reliability/security fears, and the market is now treating “software outages” as a sector-wide risk premium, not a one-off. CRM is the highest-profile cloud name in the group, so it should keep bleeding until investors see clear evidence of operational resilience and security controls. Key catalyst: continued multiple compression as peers fall and CRM’s outage narrative stays in headlines.

items.titleEn: Nebius stock is falling: Here's why NBIS may plunge to $50 soon
items.summaryEn: Sell short Nebius Group (NBIS). The article flags a technical breakdown (below $145 support, under 50/100-day EMAs, ADX ~36) plus fundamental pressure: guidance cut, hyperscaler/customer churn risk (Meta storage leasing, Microsoft reassessing), and saturated market. With AI “jitters” and potential impairments ahead, downside can extend toward the $50 level cited. Key Risk: Nebius lands a major hyperscaler deal or materially upgrades guidance, reversing the sell-off and forcing a sharp short squeeze. Short the neocloud/AI-infra peer basket via an ETF like SOXX (semis proxy for AI capex) paired with a high-beta AI infrastructure name (e.g., CoreWeave-linked exposure via public proxies) to express “AI bubble + capex pause” risk. The news points to clients prioritizing newer chips (Nvidia/Google), project delays, and Gartner-style impairments—second-order pressure hits the whole crowded buildout, not just NBIS.

items.titleEn: Micron stock falls 2%, why this analyst cut target price
items.summaryEn: Buy Micron. The article flags NAND oversupply risk, but GF Securities explicitly expects Micron’s impact to be more limited because MU has more DRAM/HBM exposure than pure-play NAND peers. If NAND prices flatten then soften, the market will over-discount MU; MU should still benefit if DRAM/HBM demand stays firmer (especially HBM tied to AI). Key Risk: DRAM/HBM demand breaks too—prices and margins fall at the same time as NAND, making MU’s “limited impact” assumption wrong. Sell SanDisk (Western Digital’s NAND business exposure). GF Securities calls it the most exposed pure-play NAND name and expects higher earnings volatility if NAND prices weaken. With consumer PC/phone NAND consumption slowing and supply expanding (including more QLC), the earnings hit should be sharper than for MU/SK Hynix.

items.titleEn: Jensen Huang keeps door open to return as Nvidia CEO in first statement since exit
items.summaryEn: Buy Nvidia (NVDA). Huang’s door-open language (“if the Board decides… in the best interest… I would return”) creates real upside optionality: markets are pricing leadership risk and governance uncertainty. If the board keeps the door cracked, sentiment can snap back ahead of/around earnings, even if reinstatement isn’t immediate. Interim CEO Colette Kress reduces operational disruption, so the main swing factor is the board’s willingness to reverse course. Key Risk: Board decides not to reinstate him and governance/China-chip access concerns keep escalating, forcing a sustained multiple compression. Sell Nvidia exposure via the most levered semiconductor supply chain: short/underweight ASML (ASML) and Applied Materials (AMAT). If NVDA’s earnings and guidance get hit by distraction, investigations, or export/geopolitical friction, capex and tool orders tied to leading-edge AI production get delayed. The CEO headline is a catalyst for near-term risk-off in AI capex expectations, which these equipment names amplify.

items.titleEn: Gold will reclaim $5,600/oz in 2028 as rate cuts bring Western investors back to precious metals – Goldman Sachs
items.summaryEn: (Kitco News) – Gold will reclaim its all-time high above $5,600 per ounce by the end of 2028 after the Federal Reserve begins cutting interest rates and Western investors return to the precious metals market, according to analysts at Goldman Sachs. In a new research note published Tuesday, analysts led by Lina Thomas said that as far as precious metals are concerned, “2027 increasingly looks like 2022.” They explained that Fed rate hikes will weigh on private investor demand for gold, even as structural central bank demand supports a firm floor beneath prices. Goldman Sachs expects to see downside risks and elevated volatility in the near term as the Fed continues to hike rates, with the investment bank’s own economists forecasting a second 25-basis-point hike in December, followed by a third in March of next year.

items.titleEn: Nike outlines $5B growth plan as turnaround faces challenges in China and sportswear
items.summaryEn: Buy NKE. The plan is specific: +$5B annual revenue by FY2031, $2.5B cost cuts, and a clear margin path to 12–14%. Even with a tough FY2027 (high-single-digit revenue decline; ~6% adjusted operating margin), the market has already punished the stock (~37% YTD). If execution hits, the rerating comes from operating leverage plus shareholder returns (~$12B dividends over five years). Key Risk: China and lifestyle demand keep deteriorating faster than Nike can cut costs and re-accelerate product momentum. Sell broad exposure to Nike-linked apparel/footwear suppliers (e.g., buy puts or short baskets of contract manufacturers and component makers tied to Nike volumes). Nike’s near-term revenue decline and margin pressure (FY2027 operating margin ~6%) typically squeeze supplier orders and pricing first, before any turnaround benefits show up.

items.titleEn: Why SpaceX stock is rising on Tuesday?
items.summaryEn: Buy. The stock is rising on two concrete catalysts: (1) a reported ~$40B Nvidia-linked AI financing structure that can rapidly expand compute capacity without loading debt onto SpaceX’s balance sheet, and (2) Nvidia increasing its stake to 130.5M shares—real money signaling confidence. Add the operational proof from Starship Flight 15: first-ever recovery of an orbital-class upper stage via the tower’s arms, which directly supports higher cadence and better unit economics. This combo is “funding + partner validation + execution,” which tends to re-rate winners fast. Key Risk: The AI/compute buildout timeline slips or the financing structure fails to deliver usable capacity on schedule, forcing SpaceX to fund growth slower and more expensively. Buy NVDA. The news is about Nvidia’s next-gen AI chips being routed through an asset-backed structure tied to SpaceX expansion. That implies stronger demand visibility and potentially faster ramp for Nvidia’s GPU shipments into the AI compute buildout. Even if the market focuses on SpaceX, NVDA is the chip supplier and the stake increase reinforces that Nvidia expects the partnership to scale.

items.titleEn: AMD shares open higher on Tuesday: here's why
items.summaryEn: Buy AMD. The World Labs + Taalas deals deepen both AI research (spatial/3D models) and inference silicon, and the OpenAI 457MW deal is a concrete demand signal for Instinct MI455X/Helios. With Intel delays and Arm not delivering the expected shift, AMD’s server CPU + accelerator share gains can compound while the stock’s valuation has already reset lower. Key Risk: OpenAI/major cloud customers delay or cancel the planned inference capacity ramp, leaving AMD’s accelerator/inference roadmap without the expected demand pull. Sell/underweight NVDA. The article flags Nvidia under pressure into its earnings, while AMD’s narrative is strengthening on inference efficiency and named hyperscaler capacity. If AI spend stays heavy but shifts toward more cost-efficient inference platforms, AMD can take incremental share and compress Nvidia’s near-term upside.

items.titleEn: Why is Intel stock falling on Tuesday?
items.summaryEn: Buy AMD (AMD). If Intel’s PC recovery stays delayed and its foundry story lacks traction, share shifts to competitors in both client CPUs and data center. AMD is the cleaner beneficiary of “Intel under-delivers” without needing Intel to fail completely—just for Intel to keep missing expectations. Key Risk: AMD’s own data-center/AI demand slows or margins compress enough that it can’t absorb share gains from Intel. Sell Intel (INTC). The news stacks: Nvidia cut its stake by 25%, Intel’s guidance misses (revenue and EPS), and the lawsuit claim adds headline risk around transparency. The market is already pricing a delayed turnaround; this filing confirms a lack of conviction from a major tech investor while PC demand stays weak and cash burn is rising.

items.titleEn: Nasdaq slips as Wall Street awaits Nvidia earnings and Anthropic IPO
items.summaryEn: Buy NVDA. The selloff is being driven by leadership drama, but the market is still anchored to NVDA’s core AI demand and platform lock-in. Even with margin/cash-flow questions, the stock is down ~24% this month—large enough that “bad news” is already priced. If earnings show stable guidance and continued strength in data-center revenue, the stock can snap back quickly. Key Risk: Earnings/guidance confirm a real slowdown in AI chip demand or a durable margin hit from cash outflows. Buy COHR and LITE. The article flags a rebound in photonics/data-center component names, and the policy angle (blocking Chinese data-center equipment) tends to shift spend toward domestic/ally supply chains. If NVDA/AI capex holds up, photonics is a direct beneficiary of higher bandwidth needs.

items.titleEn: Alibaba stock flashes the risky death cross pattern as earnings loom
items.summaryEn: Buy PDD (PDD). If Alibaba’s AI/cloud spend is crowding out near-term profitability, China’s e-commerce spend will keep shifting toward the most efficient operators. PDD has been gaining share versus weaker competitors, and it should face less “capex-to-future-earnings” discounting than BABA. In a market that’s punishing investment-heavy stories, PDD’s relative earnings durability is the edge. Key Risk: Regulators or competition force PDD to raise spending materially (or margins compress sharply), removing the efficiency advantage. Sell short Alibaba (BABA). The weekly death cross is flashing right before earnings, and the stock is below key support ($91.8) with downside targets around $80. Capex is surging (+75% YoY) while net profit is collapsing (-75% YoY), so the market has a clear “costs first, profits later” setup that can keep pressure on the multiple even if revenue holds up. The AI cloud growth (+45%) is not enough to offset margin risk given intense model competition (DeepSeek/Kimi/etc.).
